newsitem.title: SWEDEN: INTERVIEW-Atlas Copco MD sees better '97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Atlas Copco MD sees better '97.

text.p: The new head of Swedish industrial engineer Atlas Copco said he saw no reason to change the company's May forecast for a better year in 1997 despite continuing weak European markets.
"We have made our forecasts and we hope the results in the second quarter will confirm this trend to the market," managing director Giulio Mazzalupi told Reuters in an interview.

Atlas Copco forecast better results for full year 1997 compared to 1996 when the company posted an eight percent rise in profit after financial items to 3.07 billion crowns with earnings per share (EPS) of 10.56 crowns.
In the first quarter of 1997 Atlas Copco posted an eight percent drop in profits after financial items to 735 million crowns and EPS of 2.40 crowns but sales increased marginally.
The forecast for a better 1997 were despite poor European construction markets which showed no sign of a pick-up.

"There is bad news and good news in the European market," Mazzalupi said. "The bad news is that the market is really depressed at the moment. The good news is it really can't get that much worse. We have adjusted to the market conditions and are making a profit at these levels."
He projected the situation on the building market would not start to pick up before the end of 1998.
But he was more positive about other areas of the world.

"Regarding the rest of the world I am more optimistic for Asia and also for the former Soviet Union," he said. "South America looks interesting and in North America the market remains at good levels."

Mazzalupi, who replaced Michael Treschow at the helm in April, said the recent acquisition of the U.S.'s second largest equipment leasing firm, Prime Service Inc PS.N -- Atlas Copco's largest acquisition in its 124 year history -- would not have any dilution effect on EPS in the long term.
Atlas Copco had earlier said that the acquisition of Prime Service would lower the company's EPS by a maximum of five percent in 1997 and 1998.
He said the $900 million cash purchase would be good for shareholders.
"For shareholders it is good. It involves no new shares and when the company gets bigger and grows at the same pace as earlier... EPS will rise," Mazzalupi said.
Mazzalupi said Atlas Copco was always on the lookout for cost savings and better efficiency.
"You'll remember that we closed down about 15 factories over the past five years so we are through our major restructuring hardships," Mazzalupi said.
"But it is an ongoing process and not something that we see as an extraordinary measure. There'll be more of the same in the future but not in a major one-off measure."
He said the company's profitability was good.
"We have a two digit margin on turnover and we are not in a boom in the market. I see our profit level as very good."

Mazzalupi said Atlas Copco's target was the after market sector for the company's product -- leasing, fittings, and service -- which he hoped would increase to about half of the company's total turnover.
"We have too small a share of the after-market," he said.
"For the group as a whole this only accounts for about 25-30 percent of total turnover. Our ambition is that this should increase to about half."
He said it was possible that the after market sector would set up its own business area in a couple of years.
